screens.title: Dynamic Memory Allocation
screens.subtitle: Using malloc, calloc, realloc, and free to manage heap memory safely

narration.text: In this chapter we learn how programs request and return memory at runtime. You will understand the two main regions of memory—the stack used for automatic local variables and the heap used for dynamic allocations—and why the heap matters when your program needs flexible or large data structures. We'll walk through the four core functions the C standard provides for heap management: the malloc function for raw allocation, calloc for zero-initialized allocation, realloc for resizing an existing block, and free for returning memory to the system. Each function has rules and pitfalls: allocations can fail and return null, realloc may move memory, and freeing memory incorrectly can produce dangling pointers or heap corruption. The lab activity in this chapter guides you to build a dynamic integer array that grows with the user’s input, demonstrating checks for allocation failure and safe resizing. By the end you will be able to allocate and resize memory, avoid common errors like leaks and double frees, and reason about when to prefer stack or heap allocation. Keep an eye out for simple patterns that prevent bugs: always check returns, use a temporary pointer with realloc, and set pointers to null after freeing. Which allocation pattern will you use first in your next program?

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Dynamic allocation gives your program flexibility. Manage heap memory carefully to avoid leaks, crashes, and undefined behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives outline concrete skills you will practice and verify. First, you will explain why dynamic memory is necessary when the program cannot determine storage needs at compile time. This means distinguishing the stack and heap in terms of lifetime and use cases. Second, you will learn to use the four core allocation functions: the malloc function to allocate raw bytes, calloc to allocate and zero-initialize, realloc to resize a prior block, and free to return memory to the system. That knowledge includes exact calling patterns and safe idioms such as checking for null and assigning realloc results to a temporary pointer. Third, you will implement error handling that responds to allocation failures and prevents leaks. Finally, you will recognize and prevent common mistakes: forgetting to free memory, dereferencing freed pointers, and freeing the same pointer twice. Each objective ties to a practical skill: writing a dynamic array program, checking returns, resizing safely, and freeing memory responsibly. These competencies keep long-running programs stable and prevent subtle crashes. By the end you'll have verified competence in each objective through guided tasks and checks.

keyIdea.title: Measured outcomes
keyIdea.text: You will be able to allocate, resize, and free heap memory while avoiding leaks and undefined behavior.

screens.title: Stack vs Heap
screens.subtitle: Lifetimes, sizes, and when to use each region

narration.text: Start by forming a clear mental model of the stack and the heap. The stack holds function frames: local variables, parameters, and return addresses. A variable on the stack is created when its function runs and removed when the function returns; its lifetime is bound to the call. The stack size is typically limited by the system and by compile-time choices, so very large arrays or data structures are a poor fit for it. The heap, by contrast, is a larger pool of memory that you request explicitly at runtime. When you need storage whose size is unknown until the program runs—like reading user input that defines array length—you allocate from the heap and keep a pointer to that block for as long as you need it. That flexibility is powerful but also dangerous: every heap allocation must be paired with a free to avoid memory leaks. A common misconception is thinking heap memory disappears when a function returns; it doesn't. Only the pointer variable on the stack goes away if you fail to store the pointer somewhere with a sufficient lifetime. Another misconception is assuming heap allocations are inherently slower; they can be, but the important distinction is control. In practice, choose the stack for small, short-lived data and the heap for variable-sized or long-lived structures. Now consider what happens when you return a pointer to heap memory from a function and later free it correctly—this is the pattern that enables flexible data structures.

keyIdea.title: Memory regions comparison
keyIdea.text: Use the stack for temporary, small objects; use the heap for runtime-sized, persistent data, and remember to free when done.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Stack vs Heap
Core Concept

Stack and Heap compared

Understand lifetime, allocation patterns, and typical use cases so you can pick the right storage region for each data structure.

Stack: automatic lifetime, fast allocation, limited size. Good for scalars and small arrays with known size.
Heap: manual lifetime, flexible size, requires free. Good for dynamic arrays, linked structures, and long-lived buffers.
Misconception: Heap memory auto-frees when a function ends — it doesn't. You must free it explicitly.
Key Takeaway

Choose stack for brief, small storage; choose heap when size or lifetime is determined at runtime.

Annotated memory sketch
Stack (frames)
  1. Local variables and parameters
  2. Allocated and freed automatically per call
  3. Limited size, fast access
Heap (dynamic)
  1. Blocks requested with allocation functions
  2. Persist until explicitly freed
  3. Flexible size, programmer-managed
Analogy: Stack is a function's workbench that is cleared when the function finishes; the heap is a storage room you must clean up yourself.
Check your understanding: If a pointer to heap memory is stored in a global variable, will that memory be lost when a local function returns? No—only the stack frame is popped; the heap block remains until freed.

screens.title: When to use dynamic allocation
screens.subtitle: Reasons, trade-offs, and a simple decision process

narration.text: Deciding to allocate memory dynamically is a trade-off between flexibility and responsibility. Use dynamic allocation when the required size isn't known at compile time, when data must outlive a function call, or when you need large buffers that the stack cannot safely hold. The process for deciding is simple: first ask whether the data size is fixed and small—if yes, prefer stack allocation for simplicity. If size or lifetime varies, choose the heap and plan explicit deallocation. Second, consider performance and fragmentation; dynamic allocation can be slightly slower and can fragment memory over time, so use it judiciously for performance-critical code. Third, design ownership: decide which function or module is responsible for freeing each allocation. A common pattern is to have the allocator and its caller document who frees the memory. Finally, always include error handling—if an allocation fails, your code must either release other resources and exit gracefully or retry with smaller sizes. A common misconception is treating malloc as infallible; in constrained environments it can return null. Practically, follow this lightweight decision process to pick stack for simple, ephemeral objects and heap for flexible, long-lived storage, and document ownership to avoid leaks. What ownership rules will your code use?

keyIdea.title: Decision process
keyIdea.text: Prefer stack when fixed and small, choose heap for variable or long-lived data, and always document who frees memory.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › When to use dynamic allocation
Definition & Rationale

Simple decision process

1. Is the size known and small? If yes, use the stack for simplicity and performance.
2. Does the data need to live beyond the function call? If yes, allocate on the heap and return a pointer or store it in a longer-lived variable.
3. Who owns the memory? Explicitly document which part of code must free it to avoid leaks.
4. Always check for allocation failure and provide fallback behavior.
Key Takeaway

Dynamic allocation gives flexibility, but ownership and error handling are essential to avoid long-term bugs.

Process cards

Assess size and lifetime before choosing allocation region.
Design ownership: name the module that frees the memory and avoid surprises.
Plan error handling: check allocation returns and handle null safely.
Document the contract: who allocates and who frees each pointer.

screens.title: malloc — allocate raw bytes
screens.subtitle: How malloc works, return values, and size calculations

narration.text: The malloc function requests a block of bytes from the heap. It takes a single size parameter that describes the total number of bytes to allocate. Typical usage is to multiply the number of elements by the size of each element to get that total. Always check the returned pointer: a null return indicates allocation failure. A common pattern for allocating an array of integers is to compute the product of count and the size of an integer and call malloc with that value. Remember that malloc does not initialize memory; the contents are indeterminate. That means you must explicitly initialize fields before using them if you rely on specific values. Also be careful with pointer casting: in C you may assign the void pointer returned by malloc directly to a typed pointer, but many code examples cast it explicitly for clarity. A frequent error is miscomputing the size and allocating too few bytes, which can cause buffer overflows when you write past the allocated space. Another mistake is failing to check for null before using the pointer. Example: allocate space for five integers and verify the result. If allocation fails, print an error and stop or free other resources before exiting. Close with a reminder: treat malloc results as tentative until you check them, and avoid assuming memory contains zeros.

keyIdea.title: malloc checklist
keyIdea.text: Compute count * sizeof(element), call malloc, check for null, and initialize memory before use.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › malloc — allocate raw bytes
API Walkthrough

Using malloc safely

#include <stdlib.h>

int *arr;
int num_elements = 5;
arr = (int *) malloc(num_elements * sizeof(int));
if (arr == NULL) {
  printf("Memory allocation failed!
");
  return 1;
}
// arr now points to uninitialized memory for 5 integers
Compute the allocation size as elements times sizeof(element). Casting the returned pointer is common practice, though in C it's not strictly required.
Always check for null and handle failure paths to avoid dereferencing an invalid pointer.
Initialize memory before use because malloc does not zero the contents.
Common pitfalls
Incorrect size multiplication causes under-allocation and potential overflow.
Using memory before initialization can read garbage values and produce incorrect behavior.
Misusing a null pointer after allocation failure will crash the program.
Key Takeaway

Always compute sizes carefully, check for null, and initialize after malloc before use.

screens.title: calloc vs malloc
screens.subtitle: Arguments, initialization, and typical use cases

narration.text: calloc and malloc both allocate heap memory, but they differ in arguments and initialization behavior. The calloc function takes two arguments: a count of elements and the size of each element. It multiplies them and returns a pointer to a block in which all bytes are set to zero. This zero-initialization is useful when you need a clean starting state, for example when building data structures that expect zero values for fields. malloc takes a single size argument and does not initialize memory; the bytes are indeterminate. That difference can affect performance—calloc may be slower because it clears memory—but it also prevents a class of bugs caused by uninitialized reads. A typical misconception is that calloc only sets integer values to zero; in fact it sets every byte to zero, which for pointers or floating point types produces the zero bit pattern, but code should not rely on pointer bit patterns other than using null checks. Use calloc when you want guaranteed zeroed memory; use malloc plus explicit initialization when you prefer control over the initialization sequence. In either case, check for null after the call and be mindful of size calculations. Which initialization strategy fits your data layout?

keyIdea.title: calloc vs malloc
keyIdea.text: calloc zero-initializes memory and takes count and size; malloc allocates raw bytes and leaves contents uninitialized.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › calloc vs malloc

At a glance

calloc(count, size) — allocates and zeroes all bytes.
malloc(size) — allocates raw bytes with indeterminate contents.
Use calloc when you need a clean zeroed block for predictable initialization.

Example

int *arr_zero = (int *) calloc(num_elements, sizeof(int));
if (arr_zero == NULL) {
  printf("Memory allocation failed!
");
  return 1;
}
// arr_zero points to num_elements integers, all set to zero
calloc sets each byte to zero; this often results in numeric zeros for integers and predictable initial state for many structures.
Do not assume pointer bit patterns beyond using null checks; zeroed bytes may or may not correspond to a valid null pointer representation on unusual platforms.
Practical tip: choose calloc to avoid manual zeroing loops when you need all bytes cleared.

screens.title: realloc — resizing blocks safely
screens.subtitle: How realloc moves or grows memory and the safe temporary-pointer pattern

narration.text: The realloc function changes the size of an existing heap block. You pass the original pointer and the new byte size. realloc will try to resize the block in place; if it can’t, it will allocate a new block, copy the existing data into it, and free the old block. Because realloc can fail and return null, the safe idiom is to assign its result to a temporary pointer. Only if that temporary pointer is non-null should you update the original pointer. If you assign realloc’s return directly back to the original pointer and realloc fails, you lose the reference to the original block and create a memory leak. An example safe pattern is to call realloc into temp, check if temp is null, and then assign original = temp. Another important detail: when you shrink a block, some implementations may leave the trailing bytes intact but logically inaccessible; when you enlarge a block, new bytes are uninitialized unless the new memory came from a zeroed allocator. Common misconceptions include assuming realloc always preserves content beyond the original size or that it will never move the block. Always treat the returned pointer as possibly different from the original and avoid dereferencing the old pointer after a successful realloc if it returned a new address. This defensive approach keeps your program resilient to allocation failures and avoids silent leaks.

keyIdea.title: realloc safety
keyIdea.text: Use a temporary pointer for realloc, check for null, and only then update the original pointer to avoid leaks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › realloc — resizing blocks safely
Process Flow

Safe realloc pattern

1. Call realloc with the original pointer and new size into a temporary pointer.
2. If the temporary pointer is null, handle the error; the original pointer still points to the valid old block.
3. If temporary is non-null, assign the original pointer to the temporary and continue.
int *temp = (int *) realloc(arr, 10 * sizeof(int));
if (temp == NULL) {
  printf("Memory reallocation failed!
");
  // arr still valid here
} else {
  arr = temp;
}
Notes & pitfalls
realloc may move memory; always use returned pointer for subsequent access.
Do not free the original block after a successful realloc; realloc frees it when it moves data.
Never overwrite the original pointer before checking realloc's return; that is a leak risk.
Key Takeaway

Treat realloc as a potentially moving operation and use a temporary pointer to avoid losing the original block on failure.

screens.title: free — returning memory and avoiding dangling pointers
screens.subtitle: How to free memory correctly and why setting pointers to null helps

narration.text: The free function returns a previously allocated heap block to the system. Once you call free on a pointer, you must not access the memory it pointed to—doing so leads to undefined behavior and may cause crashes. A dangling pointer is a pointer that still holds a memory address whose block has been freed. A common, effective habit is to set pointers to null immediately after freeing them. That way, accidental dereferences can be detected by a null-check. Another common pitfall is calling free on the same pointer more than once. Double free can corrupt the heap allocator's internal structures and lead to crashes or unpredictable behavior. To avoid double free, design clear ownership rules: only the module that owns an allocation should free it, and once freed it should set the pointer to null or otherwise mark it invalid. Also avoid freeing pointers that were not allocated by malloc-family functions. When writing functions that accept pointers, document whether the callee will free the pointer or the caller retains responsibility. In summary: free when you're done, set pointers to null, and never free twice. These simple rules dramatically reduce a class of hard-to-debug memory errors.

keyIdea.title: free best practice
keyIdea.text: After freeing memory, set the pointer to null and follow clear ownership rules to avoid dangling pointers and double frees.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › free — returning memory
Definition

How to free safely

Call free with a pointer you previously received from malloc, calloc, or realloc.
After free, set the pointer to null to reduce the risk of accidental dereference.
Avoid freeing the same pointer twice; design ownership so only one party frees each allocation.
Key Takeaway

Free memory when you no longer need it and null the pointer to avoid dangling references and double frees.

Common-mistake card

Double free: calling free on the same pointer twice may corrupt allocator state.
Dangling pointer: reading or writing memory after free causes undefined behavior.
Freeing non-heap memory: do not free pointers to stack or static memory.

screens.title: Memory Leaks
screens.subtitle: How leaks occur and how to detect and prevent them

narration.text: A memory leak happens when allocated memory is no longer reachable by the program yet has not been freed. In short-running programs leaks may be harmless, but in long-running processes or repeated allocations they gradually consume available memory and can cause failures. Leaks typically occur when you overwrite the only pointer to an allocation, forget to free after use, or fail to free on error paths. For example, assigning a new value to an allocation pointer without freeing the previous block loses the reference to the old block and creates a leak. Detecting leaks in small programs can be manual: carefully trace allocation and deallocation points. In larger projects use tooling or runtime checks, but the simple habits are the most powerful prevention: always pair allocations with frees in a clear, documented ownership model; free in all error paths; set pointers to null after freeing; and prefer scopes where ownership is explicit. A practical misconception is assuming that returning from main will avoid leaks because the OS reclaims memory; while the OS reclaims memory on process exit, relying on that defeats good habits and breaks libraries, daemons, and embedded systems. Think about how you will free memory in success and failure paths and practice writing code that frees before every return path. Can you identify every allocation in your function and name who will free it?

keyIdea.title: Prevent leaks
keyIdea.text: Document ownership, free in all success and error paths, and avoid overwriting pointers without freeing the previous block.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Memory Leaks
Common Errors

How leaks happen

Overwriting the only pointer to an allocated block without freeing the original leads to a leak.
Forgetting to free in error paths leaves resources held even when you bail out early.
Not following ownership conventions in libraries can place the burden of free on the wrong module.
Prevention checklist: pair every allocation with a documented free, null pointers after freeing, and free on all return paths.

Scenario

If you allocate a buffer and then assign the pointer to another allocation without freeing the first, the first block is lost.
On errors, free any intermediate allocations before returning or propagate ownership cleanly.
Real-world note

Even if the OS reclaims memory on exit, disciplined freeing matters for libraries, embedded systems, and long-running processes.

screens.title: Dangling Pointers and Double free
screens.subtitle: Why they occur and concrete defensive patterns

narration.text: Dangling pointers occur when code retains a pointer to memory that has been freed. Accessing that pointer later is undefined behavior. Double free happens when free is called more than once on the same pointer, which can corrupt the heap allocator. Both errors are often the result of unclear ownership or forgetting to null pointers after free. A defensive pattern is simple: after calling free on a pointer, immediately set it to null. This makes further accidental free calls or dereferences more detectable. When designing interfaces, decide whether the caller or callee owns the memory and document that decision. For complex ownership, consider higher-level abstractions or helper functions that centralize allocation and deallocation. A contrast: freeing memory twice may crash the program immediately, while dangling-pointer access might corrupt data and cause intermittent failures. Detecting these issues in tests or during development is crucial. Use assertions or checks that pointer is non-null before freeing, and avoid freeing pointers that are not heap-allocated. The final takeaway is that clear ownership and nulling pointers after freeing eliminate many common memory bugs. Dangling Pointers and Double free means after freeing, set pointers to null, and use clear ownership rules so you never free the same block twice or access freed memory.. In practical terms, why they occur and concrete defensive patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Defensive hygiene
keyIdea.text: After freeing, set pointers to null, and use clear ownership rules so you never free the same block twice or access freed memory.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Dangling Pointers & Double free

Definitions

Dangling pointer: holds an address whose block has been freed; dereferencing it is undefined.
Double free: freeing the same block twice, which can corrupt allocator state and crash.
Defensive rule: free(ptr); ptr = NULL; and document ownership so only one party frees each allocation.

Contrast

Double free often produces immediate, reproducible crashes.
Dangling pointer bugs are often intermittent and harder to trace because memory may have been reallocated for other uses.
Key Takeaway

Nulling pointers after free and clear ownership rules prevent both dangling pointers and double frees.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: dynamic integer array
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step plan to implement allocation, resize, and cleanup

narration.text: This lab guides you through building a dynamic integer array program that demonstrates allocation, input, resizing, and cleanup. Step one: prompt the user for the initial size and call malloc with the product of count and sizeof integer. Check the returned pointer for null and, if null, print an error and exit or handle gracefully. Step two: read integers into the allocated block using the pointer like an array and print them back to confirm. Step three: prompt for a new, larger size. Use realloc into a temporary pointer and check for null. If realloc succeeds, assign the original pointer to the temporary result and read additional integers into the newly added slots. If realloc fails, the original block remains valid, so you can decide to free and exit, or ask for a smaller size. Step four: print the resized array content and then free the memory and set the pointer to null. This lab reinforces several lessons: always check allocation returns, use a temporary pointer with realloc, and free at the end. A common pitfall is forgetting to free on early error paths—remember to free any allocated blocks before returning in those cases. Which step will you pay extra attention to in your implementation?

keyIdea.title: Lab plan
keyIdea.text: Follow the allocate, use, resize with temporary pointer, and free sequence, and always check allocation returns in every path.

content.html:

Step-by-step

  1. Prompt for initial size and call malloc with size * sizeof(int); check for null.
  2. Read integers into the array and print them to verify the data was stored correctly.

  4. If realloc succeeds, read extra integers; if it fails, handle error without freeing the original pointer unexpectedly.
  5. Print all integers and finally call free and set pointer to null.

Checks and tests

Test: program frees memory on every return path.
Test: realloc uses temporary pointer and original remains valid on failure.
Test: inputs and outputs match expected counts after resizing.

The program contains TODO markers where you must call malloc, fill the array, call realloc safely, and free memory at the end. First, when allocating with malloc, compute the allocation size as the number of integers times the size of an int. After the call, check if the pointer is null; if it is, print an error and return. Second, when reading values into the array, index into the pointer like a normal array; the pointer semantics allow array-style access. Third, for realloc, store its result in a temporary pointer and check for null before updating the original pointer. If realloc fails, do not free the original block there: it remains valid. Finally, at program end, free the memory if the pointer is non-null and then set it to null. The tests for the lab will check that you handled null checks, used a temporary for realloc, and freed memory. A common misconception is believing realloc always preserves data beyond the original size; treat new bytes as uninitialized and prompt the user to fill them explicitly. As you implement each TODO, think about how errors and early returns affect allocated resources.

screens.title: Robust allocation patterns and testing
screens.subtitle: Checks, documentation, and small habits that prevent large bugs

narration.text: Adopt a small set of reliable habits to make memory management robust. First, always check the return value of malloc, calloc, and realloc for null and handle failure paths by freeing other resources and returning a clear error code or message. Second, with realloc, use a temporary pointer. Third, after free set the pointer to null to avoid dangling pointer errors. Fourth, document ownership clearly—who allocates and who frees each pointer—especially across module boundaries. Fifth, write tests that exercise failure paths by simulating allocation failures if possible, and include checks that all allocated blocks are freed at program termination in long-running scenarios. Sixth, prefer higher-level patterns when possible: localize allocations so they are freed in the same scope, or encapsulate allocation and deallocation in a helper function to centralize logic. Finally, review size calculations using sizeof on the element type rather than hard-coded byte counts to make code portable. A common misconception is that these checks are only for production code; in fact, adopting them in early exercises builds muscle memory and prevents subtle bugs later. Practice these habits and your programs will be easier to reason about and maintain. Which habit will you add to your checklist today?

keyIdea.title: Practical habits
keyIdea.text: Check returns, use temporary pointers for realloc, free and null pointers, document ownership, and test error paths.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Best Practices

Hierarchy of defensive patterns

  1. Check every allocation result for null and handle errors cleanly.
  2. Use temporary pointer for realloc and only replace original on success.
  3. Free memory once and then set pointer to null to avoid dangling and double free.
  4. Document ownership and prefer localized ownership where feasible.
  5. Write tests that exercise both success and failure paths for allocations.

Quick checklist

Size computed with sizeof(element).
realloc assigned to temp pointer then checked.
Free in all early exit and error branches.

narration.text: Keep three core ideas in mind as you work with dynamic memory. First, the heap is for runtime-sized or long-lived data; the stack is for short-lived local storage. Second, always check allocation results: malloc, calloc, and realloc can fail and return null; handle those cases gracefully. Third, follow defensive deallocation: use a temporary pointer with realloc, free memory when it's no longer needed, and set pointers to null. These three concept cards summarize the rules that prevent the most common errors: leaks, dangling pointers, and double frees. Use them as a quick checklist whenever you write code that allocates memory dynamically. keyIdea.text: Allocate only when needed, check returns, and free responsibly to avoid common memory bugs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Key Concepts
Heap vs Stack
Heap for dynamic, long-lived storage; stack for short-lived locals.
Check allocation returns
Always verify that malloc, calloc, and realloc did not return null before use.
Free and null
Free memory when done and set pointers to null to prevent dangling and double frees.
Summary
Follow these rules consistently and your code will be more reliable, easier to test, and easier to maintain.

narration.text: As a final quick reference, keep these three practical rules at hand. First, compute sizes with the element's sizeof expression rather than guessing byte counts, which avoids under-allocation. Second, assign realloc results to a temporary pointer and only update the original on success to prevent leaks. Third, free allocated memory when it's no longer needed and set the pointer to null immediately. These short reminders map directly to the lab tests and to common bugs you will encounter in real code. Use them as a short checklist before submitting or running code that allocates memory dynamically. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Key Concepts — Quick Reference
Size safely
Use sizeof on the element type when computing allocation sizes to avoid off-bytes mistakes.
realloc safely
Assign realloc's return to a temp pointer and only update the original pointer on success.
Free & null
Free memory when done and set pointers to null to avoid dangling references and double frees.
Final takeaway
Small, consistent habits in allocation and deallocation prevent the majority of dynamic memory bugs.
